notes:
I found good material from Enduring Word (Guzik), Matthew Henry, Precept Austin, the NET Bible notes, and the Bible Hub/StudyLight pages that collect the older commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Barnes, Clarke and others). I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or bibleodyssey.org, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those areas are mostly left out. The NET chapter page cut off after its note on v. 3, so I have no NET notes for vv. 4–30.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik connects this to the end of ch. 5. Moses was discouraged by what he thought was God's lack of action, and God's reply showed that He wanted Moses to know the Lord was in control of it all. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- Matthew Henry: Moses had tried what he could do and achieved nothing. Now God says Moses will see what *God* will do. The deliverance of God's church will be accomplished when God takes the work into his own hands. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- NET note: "I will do to Pharaoh" always refers to the plagues. The phrase "strong hand" could mean God's power or Pharaoh forcing Israel out. Cassuto takes the first "strong hand" as God's and the second as Pharaoh's. The NET's conclusion is that God's power was the real force behind it all. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=6)

**v. 2:** NET: "I am the LORD" looks back to the burning bush (Exod 3:15). There the name was explained by "I am that I am," meaning Yahweh is always there and never changes. Here in ch. 6 the meaning of the name will be unfolded more fully. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=6)
- Guzik: by repeating the name, God confirmed that he remained the covenant-making and covenant-keeping God, who would absolutely fulfill His promise to Moses. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)

**v. 3:** This is the key verse of the chapter. The usual evangelical view is that the patriarchs knew the *name* Yahweh but had not *experienced* what it means.
- Guzik: the patriarchs knew God as the One who made the covenant. Moses' generation would know Him as the One who keeps it. The name Yahweh appears about 160 times in Genesis. He quotes Kaiser: "The patriarchs had only the promises, not the things promised." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- NET note:
  - The Hebrew verb form means "I was not known," not "I did not make myself known."
  - "I am Yahweh" is not a new name being revealed for the first time.
  - "El Shaddai" is a title, not a name.
  - To "know" the name means to experience it. This generation would see the promises kept.

  (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=exo&chapter=6&verse=3)
- Pulpit Commentary: a name is more than a title; it is the character behind it. Jehovah seems to have been a title of God before Moses, but Moses and Israel were the first to see the side of God's character that explained and justified it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-6.html)
- Pulpit Homiletics (J. Orr): God is now showing Himself as Jehovah, "the faithful One," who remembers and fulfils his promises. The section also gently rebukes Moses: the patriarchs believed without this revelation, and Moses has been told more than they were. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/6.htm)
- Matthew Henry: the name means God finishing what He has begun. In the creation account, God is never called Jehovah until the heavens and the earth were finished (Gen 2:4). (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Expositor's Bible: the patriarchs clearly knew the name. Evidence includes the first syllable of Jochebed's name, Gen 4:26, and the place name Jehovah-jireh. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/exodus/6.htm)
- NET note on "Almighty": the meaning of *El Shaddai* is uncertain. The note finds little support for "mountain God" or "God with breasts" and sees no strong reason to doubt the ancient translation "Almighty." (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=exo&chapter=6&verse=3)

**v. 4:** Precept Austin: this restates the land promise made to Abraham in Gen 13:15 and 17:8. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**v. 5:** Henry: God takes notice of the increase of his people's calamities. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Cole (quoted at Precept Austin): "Remembered" does not mean God had forgotten. Hebrew freely describes God in human terms. A NET note quoted there says "remembering" means God is starting to act on His promises. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)
- Guzik: God had remembered His covenant; now Moses had to remember his God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)

**vv. 6–8 (the "I will" promises):** Guzik counts seven: bring out, rescue, redeem, take as My people, be your God, bring into the land, give as a heritage. He contrasts them with Satan's "I wills" in Isa 14, which Satan was powerless to carry out. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- Kaiser (quoted at Precept Austin): the verbs are in the Hebrew perfect ("past") tense, for so certain was God of their accomplishment that they were viewed as having been completed. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**v. 6:** Ellicott: the idea of God purchasing, or redeeming, Israel appears here for the first time. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-6.htm)
- "Redeem" is the kinsman-redeemer word (*go'el*), the same idea as Boaz in Ruth. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)
- Precept Austin also notes that judgment and redemption go together: Egypt had to be judged before Israel could leave, just as Christ had to become a curse for us. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**v. 7:** Precept Austin: possession is the end of redemption (1 Cor 6:20). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)
- Keil & Delitzsch see three parts in vv. 6–8: rescue from Egypt, adoption as God's nation, and guidance into the land. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-6.htm)

**v. 8:** Guzik: this is the first time Moses is told plainly to promise Israel the land, not just release from Egypt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- Guzik's Ezekiel 20 commentary links God's oath there to this verse. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-20/)

**v. 9:** Guzik: centuries of slavery made them think like slaves instead of people of the covenant; Pharaoh was bigger in their eyes than God. Kaiser pictures "anguish of spirit" as the gasping of sobbing children. Guzik also cites Ezek 20, which says Israel was worshipping Egypt's gods. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- Henry: strong passions oppose strong consolations. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Precept Austin: no signs came with these promises, only God's word, and the people would not accept it. Not listening becomes a recurring theme in the rest of Exodus. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**vv. 10–11:** Henry: God repeats his precepts before he begins his punishments. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Thompson (quoted at Precept Austin): this is blunt "exodus language," a direct demand rather than a polite request. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**v. 12:** Guzik, following G. Campbell Morgan: in ch. 4 Moses complained he lacked eloquence. Now his "uncircumcised lips" complaint comes from a sense of being unclean and unworthy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- Henry: God had already answered this objection, for the sufficiency of grace can supply the defects of nature at any time. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Courson counts this as Moses' seventh protest. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**v. 13:** Precept Austin: God simply sets aside Moses' two objections. Morris says the commission is renewed because of Moses' discouragement. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**vv. 14–15:** Cole: the narrator breaks off to identify Moses and Aaron the Hebrew way, with a genealogy. It starts with Reuben, the senior tribe, and stops once it reaches Levi. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

**vv. 16–19:** Henry: Kohath, the ancestor of the priests, was a younger son of Levi. God's favours do not go by seniority of age and priority of birth. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Constable (quoted at Precept Austin): the ages listed help confirm that Israel was in Egypt for more than 400 years. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)
- Ellicott: ages of 137, 133 and 137 would, even in Egypt, have been abnormal. (https://biblehub.com/exodus/6-20.htm)

**v. 20:** Barnes and Pulpit: marrying an aunt was lawful until Lev 18:12 forbade it. Jochebed means "glory of Jehovah," which shows the divine name was in use before the Exodus. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)
- Gill: Moses records this marriage even though it might seem to dishonour his family, because he wrote not for his own glory, but for the sake of truth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)

**vv. 21–25:** Keil & Delitzsch: the list follows the main priestly families. Aaron and Eleazar stand out because their wives are named. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)
- Benson: Amminadab was a prince of Judah, and Levites could marry into any tribe. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)
- Guzik's Numbers 25 commentary notes that the Phinehas of v. 25 is the man who later took a bold stand against Israel's sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-25/)

**vv. 26–27:** Keil & Delitzsch: in the list Aaron comes first as the elder. In the closing verses Moses comes first, as the redeemer God appointed. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)
- Henry: communion with God and serviceableness to his church are things that, above any other, put true honour upon men. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)

**vv. 28–30:** Henry: on v. 29, a faithful ambassador must declare the whole counsel of God. On v. 30, Moses seems to look back with regret on his rash words. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_006.cfm)
- Guzik: God was building endurance in Moses, the ability to keep to God's plan even when it did not seem to work. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**v. 20 (aunt or cousin?):**
- Adam Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist) says the word's meaning is uncertain. The best critics suppose that Jochebed was the cousin-german of Amram, and not his aunt. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/6-20.html)
- Poole also allows "kinswoman, or cousin, or niece." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)
- Gill (Baptist) disagrees. Num 26:59 calls her a daughter of Levi, so she must be the father's sister. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch side with Gill and say the "cousin" reading goes against how the word is used. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)

**v. 20 (is Amram Kohath's own son?):**
- Gill calls him Kohath's firstborn.
- Barnes, Pulpit and Keil & Delitzsch say he must be a later descendant with some generations left out. Keil's reason is that the Kohathites numbered 8,600 males in Moses' time. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)

**vv. 6–8 (how far the promises apply to Christians):**
- Guzik applies them directly to believers today. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-6/)
- J. Vernon McGee (dispensational) also applies them, but adds that they are specifically for Israel. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)
- On v. 7, McGee draws a Calvinist-sounding point about election before the foundation of the world. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-6-commentary)

I did not find the Lutheran, Anglican or Pentecostal teachers on these sites taking clearly different positions on this chapter.

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship (v. 3):** NET reports that Wellhausen and other source critics used this verse to argue that the "priestly source" (P) believed the patriarchs did not know the name Yahweh, while the "Yahwist source" (J) used the name throughout Genesis. NET rejects that view and lists the places in Genesis where the name is used. (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=exo&chapter=6&verse=3)

**Modern scholarship (v. 20):** the Cambridge Bible, which follows the source-critical approach, says P must here preserve a genuine ancient tradition. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/6-20.htm)

**Jewish and Christian Passover (vv. 6–7):**
- Jewish tradition links the four cups of the Passover Seder to the four "I will" statements (Mishnah Pesachim 10). (https://biblehub.com/q/Exodus_6_6_God_s_promise_to_free_Israel_2.htm)
- John MacArthur's site (gty.org) teaches the same link. (https://www.gty.org/blogs/print/B130327/celebrating-the-passover)
- Got Questions adds that Jesus used the third cup, the "cup of redemption," as the sign of the New Covenant. (https://www.gotquestions.org/Passover-Seder.html)

**Catholic translation (v. 3):** I found no Catholic commentary. The only Catholic item is a translation detail: the Douay-Rheims renders the name as "my name ADONAI I did not shew them." (https://biblehub.com/niv/exodus/6-3.htm)
